summary: A blackbody's thermal spectrum is broad and its peak wavelength shortens as temperature rises (Wien's displacement law), so a heated object first glows dull red, then orange, then white and eventually bluish-white. Classical Rayleigh–Jeans theory put B_λ ∝ k_B T/λ⁴ and diverged as λ → 0 — the 'ultraviolet catastrophe'. Planck's quantisation of oscillator energies in units of h f replaced the equipartition value with ⟨E⟩ = h f / (e^{h f/k_B T} − 1), which falls exponentially at high frequency and makes the integrated power finite.
derivation_steps: Step 1 — A blackbody is a perfect absorber that, in thermal equilibrium at temperature T, emits a continuous spectrum B_λ(λ,T) determined only by T. We want the power per unit area, per unit solid angle, per unit wavelength.

Step 2 — Classical mode counting. Electromagnetic standing waves in a cavity have 8πν²/c³ modes per unit volume per unit frequency. Equipartition assigns each mode an average energy ⟨E⟩ = k_B T, giving energy density ρ(ν) = 8πν² k_B T / c³ and spectral radiance B_λ^{RJ} = 2 c k_B T / λ⁴ (the Rayleigh–Jeans law).

Step 3 — The ultraviolet catastrophe. As λ → 0, B_λ^{RJ} ∝ 1/λ⁴ diverges. The integrated emitted power ∫₀^∞ B_λ dλ is infinite, and even a kitchen oven would radiate unbounded short-wave power — clearly wrong.

Step 4 — Planck's hypothesis (1900). The cavity's atomic oscillators can only take discrete energies E_n = n h f, n = 0,1,2,… with h ≈ 6.626×10⁻³⁴ J·s. The Boltzmann average of the mode energy is ⟨E⟩ = Σ_n n h f e^{−n h f / k_B T} / Σ_n e^{−n h f / k_B T} = h f / (e^{h f/k_B T} − 1).

Step 5 — Substitution. Replacing k_B T with ⟨E⟩ in the mode-counting result and converting ν → λ gives Planck's spectral radiance: B_λ(λ,T) = (2 h c²/λ⁵) · 1/(e^{h c/(λ k_B T)} − 1). The same h governs the photoelectric effect and the Bohr atom.

Step 6 — Two limits. For short λ (h f ≫ k_B T): e^{h c/(λ k_B T)} ≫ 1, so B_λ ≈ (2 h c²/λ⁵) e^{−h c/(λ k_B T)} → 0 — the exponential beats the 1/λ⁵, killing the UV divergence. For long λ (h f ≪ k_B T): e^{x} ≈ 1 + x, B_λ → 2 c k_B T/λ⁴, smoothly recovering Rayleigh–Jeans in the radio.
Step 7 — Peak (Wien). Setting dB_λ/dλ = 0 gives 5(1 − e^{−x}) = x with x = h c/(λ_max k_B T); numerically x ≈ 4.9651, hence Wien's displacement law λ_max T = h c / (4.9651 k_B) = b = 2.898×10⁻³ m·K.

Step 8 — Total power (Stefan–Boltzmann). Integrating B_λ over all wavelengths and solid angle gives P/A = σ T⁴ with σ = 2π⁵ k_B⁴ / (15 c² h³) ≈ 5.670×10⁻⁸ W/m²/K⁴ — a finite, T⁴ scaling, which is the second way the catastrophe is cured.

Step 9 — Why hot objects change colour. The eye sees light over ~400–700 nm. Below ~800 K the Planck peak is far in the IR and the visible tail is too weak to see (object looks black). Around 1000 K the long-wavelength tail just reaches the deep-red end: a dull cherry red. As T climbs, λ_max shortens and intensity grows rapidly in every visible band, so the perceived colour shifts red → orange (~1300 K) → yellow (~3000 K, like a tungsten filament) → white (~5500–6000 K, like the Sun's surface) → bluish-white (>10⁴ K). The shift is set by Wien's law; the brightness grows by Stefan–Boltzmann T⁴.

Step 10 — Why not green? The Planck curve is broad, not a spike. At any temperature hot enough to glow visibly, the spectrum spans most of the visible band simultaneously, so the eye integrates it and sees a desaturated 'white' that becomes bluer only as the centroid shortens. A truly green object would require a narrow-band emitter (e.g. a phosphor or atomic line), not a blackbody.
